content: The bifluoride ion, also known as the hydrogen(difluoride) ion, is represented as HF2−. This ion is a centrosymmetric triatomic anion and is notable for containing the strongest known hydrogen bond. The bond between the fluorine and hydrogen atoms in this ion has a length of 114 picometers, and the bond strength exceeds 155 kJ mol−1. A molecular orbital analysis of this ion reveals that the atoms are connected through a three-center, four-electron bond. The term hydrogen(difluoride) is written as a single word because it refers to an anionic species. If the term hydrogen difluoride were used, it would imply the existence of a neutral compound, HF2, which does not exist in reality. Certain salts containing the HF2− ion are relatively common. Examples include potassium hydrogen fluoride (KHF2). Additionally, many salts that are marketed as anhydrous sources of fluoride, such as tetra-n-butylammonium fluoride, actually contain the bifluoride ion. The bifluoride ion also plays a role in the unusually high auto-protolysis constant of liquid anhydrous hydrofluoric acid. This phenomenon is analogous to the self-ionization of water. In this process, hydrofluoric acid undergoes autodissociation. However, in this case, both the H+ and F− ions are solvated by HF molecules, so a more accurate representation of the equilibrium would involve solvated species.
